function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to create/modify.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone or push to the remote repository from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Node.js “welcome” app.  
Create a `Dockerfile` in the project root (or update it if it already exists):

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> *Why `node:18-alpine`?*  
> Alpine images are small (~50 MB) and work well for production Node apps.  
> Adjust the port (`EXPOSE 3000`) if your app listens on a different one.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Tip:**  
> Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`).  
> If you’re using Docker Hub, the image name would be `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a workflow file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to do:**
> 1. Create two GitHub secrets in the repo settings:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username (or registry username).
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token with `write:packages` scope.
> 2. If you’re using another registry (e.g. GitHub Container Registry), replace the login action and image tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new/updated files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to see what’s staged:

```bash
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the Docker image, and push it to your registry.

---

## Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional but recommended):

   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have `kubectl` configured):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Verify pods and service:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods
   kubectl get svc
   ```

---

### Recap of the files you now have

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

That’s it! 🎉 Your repo now contains everything needed to build, test, and deploy the Node.js welcome app.
